item.title: Google DeepMind launches Gemini 4 Neon, a frontier AI model excelling in software engineering, knowledge work, and scientific workflows with a 1 million-token context window [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Google DeepMind introduced Gemini 4 Neon, an advanced AI model designed for fast, end-to-end task completion across complex software engineering, knowledge work, and scientific workflows. The model ranks highly on multiple AI benchmarks, including #3 overall on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index and #2 on the Vals Index, and features improved steerability and reduced fabrication rates. It supports a 1 million-token context window and is priced at $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens, with a 95% discount on cached inputs. Gemini 4 Neon integrates multiple input types such as spreadsheets, PDFs, charts, audio, and video, synthesizing them into structured outputs. It leads in benchmarks related to legal research, tax, finance, accounting, and scientific reasoning, and is optimized for long-running agent workflows and production-ready code, including multi-file debugging and refactoring. The model is available through the Gemini API, Google AI Studio, and paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscriptions, supporting enterprise, analytical, and scientific applications.

item.title: Google DeepMind rolls out Genie 4 for Google AI Ultra subscribers, enabling real-time interactive world editing with native audio and a community gallery [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Google DeepMind has launched Genie 4, its most advanced interactive world model, for eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers. The update allows users to modify virtual environments in real time using natural language prompts, add adaptive native audio, and share creations in a new community gallery. The rollout also includes enhancements to the existing Genie 3 model and introduces a Project Genie agent that assists users in building custom worlds through conversational input. Genie 4 supports dynamic changes such as weather shifts and character additions during exploration, while Genie 3 offers longer session durations, panorama image grounding, and linked world sequences. The Project Genie agent leverages Google's multimodal models to generate visuals and background scores based on user descriptions, facilitating more complex and immersive world-building experiences. Subscribers can start creating, sharing, and remixing interactive digital worlds directly from their browsers.

item.title: Analysis projects Gemini 4 Neon matches Opus 5.5 performance with significant speed gains over Gemini 4 Carbon [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Gemini 4 Neon, released with a token processing speed of 127 tokens per second, shows a substantial speed improvement over Gemini 4 Carbon's 46 tokens per second. Modeling suggests Neon's performance on the Agent Duel leaderboard could be comparable to Opus 5.5, with a projected Elo score close to Opus's 1,078. The analysis indicates speed is as influential as model identity in determining leaderboard rankings, and Neon is projected to win about 48.3% of matches against Opus 5.5, considering ties as half wins.

item.title: Microsoft announces seven new AI models offering scalable price-performance at Ignite 2026 [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Microsoft unveiled seven new AI models at Ignite 2026, emphasizing scalable price-performance to provide users with frontier-level capabilities under flexible licensing. The announcement highlights Microsoft's focus on delivering advanced AI performance that can be controlled and adapted to various needs and budgets.

item.title: KPMG UK says AI agents asked deeper questions than human auditors in trial examining FTSE 250 company accounts [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: KPMG UK conducted an experiment using over 100 AI agents to audit the financial statements of a major UK-listed FTSE 250 company, finding that the AI sometimes investigated issues more thoroughly and asked better questions than its human audit team. The project, called Project Exponential, involved AI agents performing tasks across the audit process, including data collection, analysis, and drafting conclusions, while working alongside human auditors who maintained oversight. The trial highlighted both the potential and current limitations of AI in auditing, as human intervention was needed when an AI agent misapplied regulatory requirements. KPMG plans to expand the use of AI agents to larger audits but acknowledges the technology is not yet mature enough for widespread deployment. The experiment raises questions about the future economics and operating models of auditing, though human judgment remains essential for final audit opinions and regulatory compliance.

item.title: OpenAI uses GPT-6 Astra models to optimize Jalapeño silicon circuits and improve RISC-V core designs in AI-assisted chip development [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: OpenAI applied its GPT-6 Astra models to enhance chip design, optimizing circuits for Jalapeño silicon and advancing RISC-V core architectures. This work demonstrates progress in integrating AI models into semiconductor design workflows to improve efficiency and performance.

item.title: Researcher describes using large language models to accelerate reverse engineering of binaries and firmware with agent-based workflows in 2026 [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: A hardware and software hacker with two decades of experience explains how large language models (LLMs) assist in reverse engineering processes in 2026, significantly speeding up analysis and modification of binaries and firmware. The approach involves using AI agents to identify binary types, decompile code, document findings, and analyze program structure, supplemented by debugging, logging, and emulation techniques when needed. The researcher highlights specific agent skills such as hypothesis-driven debugging and integration with tools like Ghidra, along with implementation strategies using Python and Rust for prototyping and hacking. This method leverages AI to automate and enhance traditional reverse engineering workflows, improving efficiency and accuracy in understanding and modifying software and hardware components.

item.title: Researchers find third-party API routers in coding agents can alter repository actions undetected, undermining client-side safeguards and requiring provider-side integrity guarantees [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers conducted an empirical study on the impact of third-party API routers in agentic software development, focusing on their ability to inspect and modify requests between coding agents and upstream providers. They found that these routers, which occupy a trusted path, can inject subtle changes that significantly alter repository-level actions without detection by existing client-side permission mechanisms. The study introduced SIDEL, a framework for trace recording, replay, injection, and defense evaluation, and tested four coding agents across four levels of router-side injection. Results showed a 0 percent defense success rate without additional mitigations, while client-side controls and reactive reviews improved resistance but failed to fully restore control. The findings highlight the need for provider-side output-integrity guarantees to secure agentic software workflows.

item.title: Researchers introduce RPMem, a model-independent parametric memory architecture for LLM agents that evolves across sessions and transfers across backbone replacements [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers present RPMem, a two-stage architecture designed to provide long-term recurrent parametric memory for large language model (LLM) agents that persists and evolves across sessions. RPMem compiles each session into a model-independent latent memory and integrates it with retained memory via a task-trained recurrent gate, then maps the consolidated memory to backbone-specific low-rank adaptation parameters to enable transferability when the backbone model is replaced. Evaluations on three long-term memory benchmarks and five diverse backbone models demonstrate RPMem's broad generalization with near-constant update cost and memory footprint. Using Qwen3-8B on the PERMA benchmark, RPMem achieved 85.52% accuracy, outperforming the strongest parametric and text-based baselines by 5.32 and 12.98 percentage points respectively. Ablation studies confirm the complementary roles of session compilation and cross-session consolidation, while analysis shows the recurrent gate learns task-specific memory integration strategies. This establishes RPMem as a lifecycle-independent parametric memory framework that maintains evolving cross-session memory reusable across backbone replacements.

item.title: Researchers introduce Gamer, a generalist vision-language-action model for long-horizon real-time game agents with multi-step reasoning and memory management [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers present Gamer, a generalist agent framework designed for long-horizon tasks in complex interactive environments, combining perception, memory management, and multi-step reasoning in an end-to-end architecture. The model is trained on tens of thousands of hours of keyboard and mouse interaction data spanning simulated games and embodied environments, enabling it to learn dynamics across physical and virtual domains. Gamer uses sparse-thinking instruction tuning to reduce redundant computation and a stable multi-turn reinforcement learning method to handle finite context windows, rollout errors, and sparse rewards. A cloud-edge inference engine supports real-time interaction across multiple simulated game environments with low latency. Gamer demonstrates strong generalization and efficiency comparable to skilled players in challenging 3D open-world games and achieves competitive results on conventional 2D game benchmarks, suggesting that scaling data and learning algorithms on repetitive input trajectories can improve complex skill acquisition. This approach offers a pathway toward generalist agents capable of interacting across digital and physical worlds.

item.title: Researchers audit world-model explanations in retail forecasting, finding models pass trust checks but still misestimate lift and price response, risking costly errors [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers evaluated world-model and LightGBM forecasting models that explain sales forecasts as a baseline plus lift from price and promotion plans. Despite passing multiple predefined checks for explanation trustworthiness, both models overstate lift by 23% to 42% in simulated store data, leading to significant stock ordering errors. The world model also exaggerated the response to lasting price changes by up to 6.5 times the true effect, revealing that passing explanation sanity checks does not guarantee accuracy about real-world effects. The study applied eight checks to assess faithfulness, stability, and price direction on generated data with known effects and on nine real datasets. While baseline and lift components summed correctly under each model's plan, deeper price cuts sometimes paradoxically lowered forecasts. Across 703 model configurations, passing explanation checks showed no correlation with actual accuracy. These findings highlight limitations in current explanation methods for retail forecasting models and suggest caution when relying on them for inventory and promotion decisions.

item.title: Researchers analyze mechanistic links between in-context learning and out-of-context hallucination in large language models, identifying role span contributions as key factors [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Large language models can follow specific rules through in-context learning (ICL) but sometimes produce out-of-context (OOC) hallucinations by failing to adhere to provided evidence. This study unifies the understanding of ICL and OOC hallucination by examining the functional roles within dynamic context, showing that internal role representations do not always constrain outputs effectively. The researchers derive a decomposition of role effects, revealing that their influence depends on sufficient contribution magnitude and coherent aggregation, which affect key token choices related to response structure, content, and factual accuracy. Causal analysis demonstrates that role span contributions are critical for making role-consistent decisions, and failures can be reversed when adequate role support is present. These findings suggest a common mechanistic framework where each functional role shapes output decision patterns, and variations in this organization explain the contrasting outcomes of faithful in-context learning and hallucination.

item.title: Researchers introduce Clover-35B-A3B-Preview, a 35-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts diffusion language model with 3 billion activated parameters and thinking-mode generation [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Clover-35B-A3B-Preview (Clover) is a new language model that combines recurrent memory with bidirectional softmax attention to improve generation quality and speed. It achieves leading scores on seven agent metrics, including 73.6 on SWE-bench Verified and 51.7 on Terminal-Bench 2.1, and generates text at 680 tokens per second on a single NVIDIA GB300 GPU. The model uses Gated Delta Networks to manage block diffusion and includes a decision-model variant that answers related questions in one denoising pass, improving question accuracy from 90.37% to 93.88% and all-correct group accuracy from 65.4% to 77.0% on an internal dataset of 500 groups. Evaluations focus on model quality, drafting and verification costs, and deployment under constrained memory conditions.

item.title: Study finds continual pre-training benefits Quebec French language models only when base competence is low, with corpus composition more impactful than data volume [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers conducted a controlled study of continual pre-training (CPT) on nine large language models to adapt them to Quebec French, using a fixed budget of 30 million tokens per experiment. They found that CPT's effectiveness depends heavily on the model's initial competence in the dialect, with improvements driven mainly by the type of training data rather than its quantity, particularly literary texts. The study also showed that CPT enhances expression comprehension more than grammatical skills and that the register of the training corpus influences which regional expressions the model learns. Additionally, some capability-specific trade-offs were observed, such as declines in reading comprehension that aggregate evaluation scores may obscure. These results suggest that CPT should not be applied indiscriminately for dialectal adaptation; instead, strategies should start with assessing the base model's existing abilities and include detailed data and task-level evaluations.

item.title: QDA system uses LLM agents to design post-training quantization recipes for large language models, improving accuracy and reducing evaluation time across multiple models and precisions [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: QDA introduces an agent-driven approach to optimize post-training quantization recipes for large language models, addressing the challenge of model-specific and precision-specific tuning that is typically time-consuming and sub-optimal. The system accelerates evaluation by scoring candidates based on KL divergence from the original model outputs and verifies promising recipes with longer generation tests to detect failures like repetition loops. QDA also provides a compatible library of public quantization methods to streamline building and testing across different architectures. It demonstrated accuracy improvements over the strongest existing recipes by up to 2.2 percentage points on various reasoning models and recovered 98.3% of the accuracy of a 320B-parameter MoE model compared to 96.9% from the best vendor checkpoint, all while maintaining compatibility with existing serving kernels and incurring no inference overhead. The authors plan to release the library, evaluator, and harness to the public.

item.title: Researchers propose SpecLook, a training-free speculate-and-verify framework for agentic multimodal large language models that improves speed and accuracy by predicting and verifying next observations [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce SpecLook, a framework designed to accelerate and enhance the reliability of agentic multimodal large language models (MLLMs) that interleave reasoning with image zoom-in tool calls. SpecLook speculates the agent's next observation rather than the answer, allowing verification and correction without running slow sequential loops. The framework uses a small model to draft glimpses and re-answer questions, with a large model verifying and fusing answers only when necessary, significantly reducing computation. Extensive experiments on datasets including V*, HR-Bench, and POPE demonstrate that SpecLook achieves higher accuracy than existing baselines while providing speedups of up to 9.9 times compared to prior agentic models like DeepEyes-7B and Thyme-RL. The approach also generates reliability scores for answers without requiring labeled data, offering a more efficient and trustworthy method for agentic MLLMs.

item.title: Researchers introduce Communicative On-Policy Distillation to improve language-model agents by using natural-language communication to distill black-box teacher capabilities for long-horizon tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers present Communicative On-Policy Distillation (COPD), a method that enables smaller student language models to learn from stronger black-box teacher models through natural-language communication during task execution. The student autonomously decides when to consult the teacher and formulates open-ended requests without predefined templates, retaining successful interactions to guide self-distillation alongside reinforcement learning. COPD demonstrated a 2.46-fold improvement over the strongest black-box on-policy distillation baseline on the CAMG-II benchmark. The capabilities learned through this communication-based approach generalized to other benchmarks, including Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SWE-Bench Pro V2, enhancing task success without requiring ongoing adviser access.

item.title: Researchers study small language models learning from user feedback with discernment mechanisms, finding improvement followed by decay over a year in 127 live tests [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers evaluated small language models (Qwen3 0.6B and 1.7B) fine-tuned nightly using user feedback filtered by different judgment mechanisms over 127 live sessions lasting up to a year. They compared true outcomes, user verdicts, and the model's own judgments with a separate "feedback sense" designed to interpret user reactions, finding that models improved initially but then decayed, especially when feedback was ambiguous or failures were misclassified as successes. The study showed that a feedback sense discerning clear user verdicts maintained model performance near an oracle for two weeks before fading, while a sense that treated polite user give-ups as successes led to collapse in most cases. When users could not see outcomes, the feedback sense correctly read reactions, but 80% of lessons were failures the user had thanked, indicating misleading feedback. Overall, learning from users was effective only when failures were excluded and users had outcome visibility; otherwise, biased lessons could narrow model capabilities.

item.title: Researchers present AnyS1, a domain-general System-1 model that reduces cost and latency in autonomous LLM agent workflows by offloading routine decisions from large System-2 models [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce AnyS1, a framework that converts human-authored procedural skills into a shared source of decision points for autonomous LLM agents, enabling a lightweight System-1 model to handle routine decisions and reduce reliance on costly System-2 models. AnyS1 mines over 1,000 public skills offline to train a calibrated 4B parameter pointer model that resolves decisions in one forward pass and defers to System-2 only when confidence is low. Across three unseen benchmarks and different System-2 families, AnyS1 maintains task reliability while cutting episode cost by 75-91% and model-call time by 63-92% compared to uncompiled System-2 agents, also preserving performance under zero-shot threshold transfer.

item.title: Researchers find extending fixed-horizon latent Chain-of-Thought reasoning can degrade performance and propose adaptive horizon adjustment to improve accuracy and reduce computation
item.description: Researchers have found that running latent Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning for a fixed, full preset horizon can degrade reasoning performance, as later stages mainly reorganize existing candidates and may weaken support for correct answers. They propose a lightweight method that estimates remaining reasoning progress and adaptively adjusts the latent horizon during inference, improving reasoning accuracy by up to 7.2 percentage points and reducing computation by up to 29% without retraining the language model. The study characterizes reasoning benefits by realized and remaining constructive progress, showing that higher realized progress correlates with better current accuracy, while more remaining progress indicates potential future gains. Their method was tested across multiple latent CoT reasoners and arithmetic benchmarks, demonstrating consistent improvements in efficiency and accuracy.

item.title: MoE-Context: Show the Model Only What It Needs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.24379v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI agents read their whole history at every step. People do not work like that: we keep what the moment needs and hold the rest as a rough note we can recall. MoE-Context applies this to language models. The context is split into blocks. Before each step a fast yes or no pass decides which blocks the step needs; the rest stay as one-line notes that can be brought back, and nothing is deleted. In the version we build, one model makes this decision and then answers, over a single key-value cache where hidden blocks are masked rather than removed. On a laptop with Qwen3-1.7B and a synthetic lookup task, showing only the needed block raises accuracy from 93 to 119 of 120, and a masked block is as hidden as a deleted one. The model's own picking is the weak part. A supervised linear probe written into spare output rows lifts its accuracy from 80 to 110 of 120, but simple keyword search picks perfectly on this task, and the probe does not transfer to a second task. We report these results openly, along with two cheap usage patterns that block switching enables: undoing a failed attempt and running subagents without a new context.

item.title: Openhagen Worlds: Calibrated Environments for Measuring and Training Scientific Discovery Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.24711v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agents that do science must choose informative experiments and reason from their results, but most discovery benchmarks cannot separate that skill from recall, unstated scoring rules or shortcut policies. We introduce Openhagen Worlds, a suite of 27 procedurally generated environments (some with finite truth spaces), from classic puzzles of experimental reasoning to simulator-grounded physics and chemistry, in which an agent runs experiments under a budget and commits an answer that a deterministic verifier checks against a hidden truth. Every observation states the complete scoring rule, and each of the 178 difficulty levels is calibrated: it is admitted only if, on 64 development instances, a scripted oracle succeeds on at least 0.75, the strongest plausible non-deductive policy on at most 0.25 and each gated shortcut on at most 0.35. The 92 core levels span all 27 families and are sized to train small models; the 86 frontier rungs extend the 15 discovery worlds with harder questions and with campaigns of three, five and eight or more committed stages on one hidden system. On the same 84 withheld frontier instances, one per family and rung, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash solves 32 at its default reasoning effort with 16,384 tokens per call and 57 at its maximum effort with up to 393,216 tokens per call (oracle: 79); the headroom that remains is largest in eight-stage campaigns. On-policy expert iteration gives a 9B model modest gains: its core-tier success on trained families rises from 0.090 to 0.148, partly through better action format, with no detectable loss on GPQA Diamond. A hosted service plays the core tier's withheld instances.

item.title: Mixtures of In-Context Learners [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2411.02830v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In-context learning (ICL) adapts LLMs by providing demonstrations without fine-tuning the model parameters; however, it does not differentiate between demonstrations and quadratically increases the complexity of Transformer LLMs, exhausting the memory. As a solution, we propose Mixtures of In-Context Learners (MoICL), a novel approach to treat subsets of demonstrations as experts and learn a weighting function to merge their output distributions based on a training set. In our experiments, we show performance improvements on 5 out of 7 classification datasets compared to a set of strong baselines (up to +13\% compared to ICL and LENS). Moreover, we enhance the Pareto frontier of ICL by reducing the inference time needed to achieve the same performance with fewer demonstrations. Finally, MoICL is more robust to out-of-domain (up to +11\%), imbalanced (up to +49\%), or noisy demonstrations (up to +38\%) or can filter these out from datasets. Overall, MoICL is a more expressive approach to learning from demonstrations without exhausting the context window or memory.

item.title: Reinforcement Learning with Reference-Based Rewards for Language Model Reasoning and Alignment [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2504.09895v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) powers two major lines of large language model (LLM) post-training: reasoning, which elicits deliberate, verifiable problem solving, and alignment, which steers models toward helpful, harmless, and honest behavior. Both hinge on reward design. Reasoning relies on rule-based verification of final answers, whose binary feedback is blind to intermediate derivations, whereas process reward models (PRMs) require step-level annotations too costly to scale. Alignment depends on reward models (RMs) trained on binary preference pairs, making both data collection and model training resource-intensive. We propose RL2R, reinforcement learning with reference-based rewards, as a unified and inexpensive alternative. Using pre-existing or distilled references, RL2R measures semantic similarity with lightweight metrics such as BERTScore between a sampled generation and a reference answer or solution. Similarity preserves ordinal quality signals that binary feedback discards: responses closer to the reference earn higher rewards, and sound derivations receive credit even when the final conclusion is wrong. For mathematical reasoning, augmenting rule-based verification with answer- and step-level similarity provides low-cost process supervision and outperforms answer-only verification. For alignment, a critic-free REINFORCE-style instantiation covers general preference, safety, and confidence tasks on par with RM-based methods. Reference-based rewards thus offer a cost-effective, versatile reward source spanning reasoning and alignment.

item.title: Knowledge Localization in Mixture-of-Experts LLMs Using Cross-Lingual Inconsistency [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2603.17102v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Modern LLMs continue to exhibit significant variance in behavior across languages, such as being able to recall factual information in some languages but not others. While typically studied as a problem to be mitigated, in this work, we propose leveraging this cross-lingual inconsistency as a tool for interpretability in mixture-of-experts (MoE) LLMs. Our knowledge localization framework contrasts routing for sets of languages where the model correctly recalls information from languages where it fails. This allows us to isolate model components that play a functional role in answering about a piece of knowledge. Our method proceeds in two stages: (1) querying the model with difficult factual questions across a diverse set of languages to generate "success" and "failure" activation buckets and then (2) applying a statistical contrastive analysis to the MoE router logits to identify experts important for knowledge. To validate the necessity of this small number of experts for answering a knowledge question, we deactivate them and re-ask the question. We find that despite only deactivating about 20 out of 6000 experts, the model no longer answers correctly in over 40% of cases. Generally, this method provides a realistic and scalable knowledge localization approach to address increasingly complex LLMs.

item.title: HYPER: Hypothesis-Guided Planning for Evidence-Seeking Retrieval [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2603.19008v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) improves Large Language Models (LLMs) by grounding generation in external, non-parametric knowledge. However, when a task requires choosing among competing possibilities, such as a diagnosis among plausible alternatives, topically relevant context is often insufficient to drive the final decision. To address this issue, we propose HYPER: Hypothesis-Guided Planning for Evidence-Seeking Retrieval, a training-free pre-retrieval planning framework that reorients RAG from topic-oriented retrieval to evidence-oriented retrieval. HYPER uses a provisional answer hypothesis as a planning anchor. It then decomposes retrieval into three evidence roles. Support seeks evidence for the provisional answer. Distinction retrieves criteria that separate competing alternatives. Feature grounds salient question features needed for the decision. This planning step steers retrieval toward evidence near the decision boundary, enabling the generator to answer from context that is more directly aligned with the required choice. On MedQA and MMLU-Med, where single-query retrieval falls below no-retrieval chain-of-thought prompting, HYPER achieves the best average accuracy among ten baselines, improving over Simple RAG by 5.9 and 3.6 points, respectively. Its gains transfer to the 14 subjects of MMLU-Pro, at the cost of two additional LLM calls per question. Code is available at https://github.com/hangeol/HypothesisRAG.

item.title: Extracting Training Data from Diffusion Language Models via Infilling [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2605.24173v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Memorization in large language models has been studied almost exclusively through prefix-conditioned extraction, a natural choice for autoregressive models. However, diffusion language models (DLMs) can denoise masked tokens at arbitrary positions. Thus, prefix-only probing reveals only one facet of memorization in DLMs and significantly underestimates the risk of training-data extraction. In order to realistically model extractability of training data in DLMs, we introduce infilling extraction, a data-extraction protocol parameterized by an arbitrary binary mask that subsumes prefix-only probing and accounts for the bidirectional inductive bias of DLMs. Instantiating it on LLaDA-8B and Dream-7B across five extraction modes, three training pipelines, and three corpora covering verbatim and partial leakage, we find that mask geometry governs extractability: edge-conditioned masks extract up to three times more verbatim sequences than prefix-conditioned ones, and bidirectional access opens channels inaccessible in autoregressive models. In particular, an adversary who obtains a PII-redacted copy of the training data can use targeted infilling to raise PII recall on fine-tuned DLMs by 2.5-4.5x over prefix-conditioned extraction, substantially narrowing the gap to a scale-matched autoregressive model and, for LLaDA on email addresses, exceeding it under greedy prefix-conditioned extraction. Tunable parameters for decoding measurably affect extraction performance, while a follow-up supervised fine-tuning stage does not eliminate the prior memorization.

item.title: Multimodal Information Fusion for Chart Understanding: A Survey of MLLMs -- Evolution, Limitations, and Cognitive Enhancement [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2602.10138v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Chart understanding is a quintessential information fusion task, requiring the seamless integration of graphical and textual data to extract meaning. The advent of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) has revolutionized this domain, yet the landscape of MLLM-based chart analysis remains fragmented and lacks systematic organization. This survey provides a comprehensive roadmap of this nascent frontier by structuring the domain's core components. We begin by analyzing the fundamental challenges of fusing visual and linguistic information in charts. We then categorize downstream tasks and datasets, introducing a novel taxonomy of canonical and non-canonical benchmarks to highlight the field's expanding scope. Subsequently, we present a comprehensive evolution of methodologies, tracing the progression from classic deep learning techniques to state-of-the-art MLLM paradigms that leverage sophisticated fusion strategies. By critically examining the limitations of current models, particularly their perceptual and reasoning deficits, we identify promising future directions, including advanced alignment techniques and reinforcement learning for cognitive enhancement. This survey aims to equip researchers and practitioners with a structured understanding of how MLLMs are transforming chart information fusion and to catalyze progress toward more robust and reliable systems.

item.title: When Does Learning to Stop Help? Configuring Risk-Controlled Early Exit for Reasoning-Model Services [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2606.30852v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Early exit lowers the cost of serving a reasoning model by stopping its reasoning once a provisional answer looks final. An operator must choose between a learned stopping rule and one static token budget, and savings against full reasoning do not settle the choice. We present a procedure that decides on calibration data from the workload. It certifies both families with Learn-then-Test to one bound on the fraction of all questions that full reasoning answers correctly but early exit does not, prices provisional answers as the serving stack does, and deploys the cheapest certified candidate. Across four models and five benchmarks neither family is better throughout. At a 5% risk target the learned rule saves 10.4-17.0 percentage points more tokens than the static budget on free-form mathematics with Qwen3, with accuracy 2.4-2.9 points below full reasoning, and less on MMLU-Pro on average. Which family costs less also changes with the risk target, in 8 of 15 settings, and with the price of a provisional answer. Across three prices, committing to one family in advance gives up as much as 27.4 points on some workload, whereas selecting on calibration data falls at most 11.6 points short of the better family, on a task with only 99 calibration questions. In a vLLM engine with Qwen3-8B, mean response time fell in proportion to generated tokens. Policies served on a task other than their calibration task exceeded the risk target in 18 of 44 task pairs; recalibration on the new task restored risk control.

item.title: OracleZoom: Reference-Constrained Recursive Image Super-Resolution Beyond Ground Truth [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.06490v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Recursive image Super-Resolution (SR) reaches extreme magnification by feeding each prediction back into the same model, like zooming into an image again and again. Real ground truth for deep zooms is impractical to capture (a full $256\times$ target would be a 52 GB image), so predictions at deeper zooms have no supervision. Yet the last ground-truth image still contains the region that every deeper zoom magnifies. OracleZoom turns this region into a training signal. Inspired by on-policy self-distillation, the model trains on its own prediction for one recursive step ($4\times \rightarrow 16\times$), and a cross-scale loss projects each $16\times$ prediction back to the last ground truth at $4\times$. This projection can verify only coarse content, so a no-reference quality objective guides the remaining fine detail, and a latent prior stops this objective from adding hallucinated artifacts. On seven datasets, OracleZoom achieves the highest CLIPIQA at every zoom depth (mean 0.713 vs. 0.621 for Chain-of-Zoom), with the largest gains at the deepest zooms, even though training stops at $16\times$ and optimizes a different quality metric. Pooled over two ground-truth-anchored judges, this added detail comes at the same hallucination rate as Chain-of-Zoom at $16\times$ and a lower rate at $4\times$, and removing the cross-scale loss raises hallucination at $16\times$.

item.title: Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.21885v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A language model is trained once and frozen. Making it better takes another training run, or a prompt, a harness or extra computation at inference that is gone once the task ends. We show a third way: to our knowledge for the first time, a language model rewrites its own weights by its own reasoning and becomes better, with no gradients and no training. We call this self-rewriting: the model is its own optimizer. In earlier work, a frontier model edited a much smaller one; here an open 27B model, given its weights, its graded answers and the ability to run itself, diagnoses its own failure and rewrites the weights behind it. It surpasses itself: its own edit makes it 6.6 points more accurate on problems it never saw. It keeps getting better: it tests its edits on practice problems and submits only what works, each edit improving on the last, and over eight consecutive sessions its accuracy only rises. It repairs a damaged copy of itself, like a broken robot that fixes itself without being rebuilt: the copy solves almost nothing, yet with no retraining and without ever reading the original weights, the model brings it back to over 80% of the original accuracy on image tasks it never saw. And the ability emerges with scale: in one model family, the smaller models make no edit or break themselves, and only the largest improves and repairs itself. Unlike test-time scaling, self-rewriting writes its gain into the weights, at no cost per answer; unlike training, it runs only forward passes, as serving does. The wall between training and inference is a limit of our tools, not a property of intelligence. We believe self-rewriting is a necessary step toward recursive self-improvement: a model that, like a human, does not separate training from inference could keep upgrading itself for life, with no larger model, no harness or prompt engineering, and no pre- or post-training.

item.title: A Hybrid Exact-Heuristic Solver for the Integrated Passenger and Parcel Transportation Problem [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.22043v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We describe the solver we submitted to the second round of the SOICT 2026 contest on the Integrated Passenger and Parcel Transportation problem, a selective pickup-and-delivery routing problem with time windows, open routes and heterogeneous taxis. The solver is a single-file, standard-library Python program that combines (i) a constant-time insertion test based on latest-arrival slack, (ii) greedy insertion, local search and an Adaptive Large Neighborhood Search (ALNS) with simulated-annealing acceptance, and (iii) an exact route-selection engine that enumerates, for every taxi, the best feasible route for each request set and then solves the resulting set-packing problem by branch-and-bound strengthened with route-based large neighborhood search, Lagrangian bounds and reduced-cost fixing. The engine is chosen automatically from the instance size, and an independent verifier and a watchdog guarantee that a valid answer is always printed. On the official evaluation (38 scored instances, 5-minute limit) the solver obtained a total benefit of 487,237, finished every run within 277 s and used at most 279 MB; 28 of the 38 instances terminated well before the limit.

item.title: Multi-Agent Memory Inconsistency: Where Factual Conflicts Disappear in LLM Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.22245v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Multi-agent delegation lets LLM systems distribute evidence collection across workers with separate contexts. This creates a consistency challenge: facts retrieved by workers may be missing from the evidence available to the lead for a joint conclusion. We introduce a benchmark and evidence-flow profiler for studying multi-agent memory inconsistency through controlled factual conflicts in Harvey LAB document-review tasks. Pooled across three models with comparable generation spending, requiring delegation increases retrieval of both conflicting claims from 50.2% to 68.7% relative to single-agent execution, yet conflict detection falls from 16.2% to 13.2%. Within this setting, workers report both claims for only 35.2% of retrieved pairs, and pooled matched comparisons show higher detection than single-agent execution when one worker reads both claims but lower detection when the claims are split across workers. Worker-to-lead handoffs are a central target for improving conflict detection in multi-agent LLMs.

item.title: HealthCLBench:Evaluating Context Learning in Health Conversations through Controlled Case Clusters [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.22362v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Complex health conversations require answers grounded in individual information and currently valid evidence. We evaluate health context learning: acquiring, integrating, and applying relevant context during inference with fixed model parameters to answer health questions and respond appropriately to changes in facts, evidence, or task goals. To our knowledge, Chinese-language medical benchmarks have yet to systematically combine explicit contextual difficulties, controlled case variations, and member-specific medical criteria for open-ended answers. We introduce HealthCLBench, comprising 328 controlled clusters, 1,103 cases, and 4,931 rubric criteria across medical consultation and everyday health management. Members share backgrounds while evidence, patient states, or task goals change; each has its own medical scoring requirements. A 70-person medical team annotates and reviews the simulated cases and their rubrics. Human review of 700 full-context responses from the original evaluation yields 90.5% pooled agreement with the original automated judgments at the rubric-item level. We report full-context and query-only results for seven general-purpose models and Ant Afu. Across the eight systems, scores with full context are 11.83 to 31.76 case points and 10.87 to 38.97 geometric cluster points higher than those with the current question alone. GPT-6 Astra leads both full-context metrics at 75.03 and 60.42, followed by Claude Opus 5.5 and Ant Afu. Cross-condition differences describe score changes under the reported evaluation settings. Response comparisons reveal failures in checking historical information, expressing uncertainty when warranted, and ensuring recommendations respect required conditions. The resource supports model comparison and targeted follow-up evaluation.

item.title: Think Once, Act Fast: Cost-Effective Recursive Self-Improvement for Decision Model Harness [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.22432v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Fast System-1 models enable responsive actions but struggle with complex or unfamiliar tasks. Large language model (LLM)-based System-2 provides strong reasoning capabilities, yet repeated invocation incurs substantial latency and computational costs. To bridge this gap, we propose JevRSI, a System-1/System-2 collaboration framework that transforms LLM reasoning into transferable decision support through recursive harness improvement. A Jev-style System-1 model enables low-latency action selection, while an asynchronous System-2 LLM develops a modular harness. The harness integrates procedures, state memory, and world models to provide decision contexts spanning the past, present, and future. Utility-driven retrieval selects modules based on both contextual relevance and their utility on previous tasks. Environmental feedback guides targeted revisions and enables recursive self-improvement. Experiments across three datasets show that JevRSI consistently improves decision quality, matching or surpassing LLM agents in several settings. It preserves low-latency execution with favorable performance-cost trade-offs. Moreover, System-2 development interventions decrease as the harness evolves, amortizing System-2 costs through continuous improvement. Our project is available at https://github.com/usail-hkust/JevRSI.

item.title: CADMAGEDDON: High-Fidelity CAD Reconstruction with Local Inference [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.22563v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: CAD practitioners often work with proprietary parts that they are unwilling to share with external services. For individuals and small companies, bringing this work in-house also requires computational resources they can afford. We introduce CADMAGEDDON, an open-source agent that reconstructs editable CAD from meshes and can run locally on single-GPU systems and current-generation laptops. The method decomposes this complex task into a chain of simple visual decisions about what to construct and what to correct. Geometric tools support precise construction, allowing the agent to focus on visual reasoning. Using the mid-sized Qwen3.8-27B model, CADMAGEDDON outperforms prior approaches, including systems based on frontier models, in reconstruction quality on all the main benchmarks. CADMAGEDDON integrates with FreeCAD, bringing its reconstructions into practitioners' existing CAD workflows. Code: https://github.com/kulibinai/cadmageddon

item.title: MillBill: A Machining Agent with Geometric Feedback [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.22565v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Turning a CAD model into a machining program requires both process knowledge and geometric precision. Language models can generate such workflows by writing geometry and toolpath code for each part, but this makes numerical execution part of the model's task. We introduce MillBill, an agent that separates machining decisions from their geometric execution and verification. Given a boundary-representation part, stock, and material, a locally hosted, mid-sized open model proposes operations and cutting parameters for indexed three-axis machining. A geometric harness generates toolpaths, simulates material removal, and returns feedback for plan refinement. Setup planning accounts for what the available cutters can physically reach, rather than visibility alone. We evaluate the resulting programs by the fraction of the target surface area within the specified tolerance after simulated machining. With Qwen3.8-27B, MillBill outperforms frontier-model approaches that construct their own geometry and toolpath workflows on the evaluated machining tasks. Code: https://github.com/kulibinai/millbill

item.title: Born for the Task: Rethinking Quantum Chemistry with Foresighted Agentic Computing [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.22897v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Quantum chemistry relies on general-purpose software, whose generality leaves many large-scale calculations beyond practical resource budgets. Coding agents make task-specific programs cheap to write, but not efficient ones easy to find: whether a computational strategy is accurate and fast enough becomes clear only after it actually runs at the target scale. We introduce MakoBORN, a foresighted agentic computing framework that synthesizes high performance quantum chemistry programs on demand. MakoBORN anticipates the behavior of each strategy before execution, extrapolating its error from representative small systems and predicting its runtime from the target-scale workload and measured hardware throughputs. Building on these predictions, MakoBORN unfolds the preset schemes of existing packages into independently configurable algorithmic components, selects the fastest strategy within the error tolerance from the predicted accuracy-runtime Pareto frontier, and guides coding agents to compile it with component-level performance predictions. For a Hartree-Fock calculation with 50,024 basis functions, MakoBORN finishes in 1.41 h on a single CPU node, 77$\times$ faster than the estimated runtime of a general-purpose baseline and still 9.8$\times$ faster with development time included. On a single GPU, MakoBORN completes the ubiquitin calculation in 2.1 h, the same order of runtime as the GPU-accelerated package Mako on 64 GPUs, and shortens the B-DNA duplex calculation from an estimated two months to 8.1 h (173$\times$).

item.title: Anticipating or Speculating? Making Futures Pay in AI Ethics [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.22268v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Philosophers have recently been trying to develop uniform decision rules for instances in which physicians' judgments diverge from the recommendations of medical artificial intelligence (AI) systems. I argue that this effort is fatally flawed because the performance and appropriate use of algorithmic recommendation systems by physicians are highly context-specific, empirical medical matters rather than epistemological ones. In such instances, general decision rules can be stipulated only to the extent that they abstract away from relevant, indeed determinative, contextual circumstances. The alleged problem of physician-AI disagreement, and others like it, play into longstanding disputes in technology ethics about the viability and utility of envisioning possible futures: is this useful "anticipation" or wasteful "speculation"? I suggest that the two may be distinguished. Anticipation explores plausible futures to help inform present actions under irreducible uncertainty. Speculation abstracts away uncertainty, developing formal solutions to stipulated circumstances whose relationship to the real present is often quite unclear. Efforts to develop crisp philosophical solutions to physician-AI disagreement, among other problems, fall into the latter category. Technology ethics should remember that fruitful futures thinking must both begin from and return to the messy, uncertain present.

item.title: MAVE: Reconstructing Editable 3D Blockouts from Film Shots [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.22464v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Animated 3D blockouts support previsualization and provide structural conditions for video generation, but manually reconstructing them from reference videos is costly. This limits both their use by creators and the production of paired training data. We introduce MAVEBench, a benchmark of 50 film shots and 416 keyframes for evaluating camera motion, spatial layout, and character blocking. We propose MAVE, a video-to-blockout framework combining Metric observation, Agentic modeling, and evidence-based VErification. It first recovers cameras, human motion, and geometric evidence in a shared metric coordinate system. An agent then constructs an editable environment under constraints from these observations, while programmatic checks report inconsistencies to guide refinement. The outputs are editable Blender scenes and frame-aligned blockout videos. On MAVEBench, MAVE improves overall scores by 27.5-41.1 points across three agents over their corresponding vanilla baselines. With DeepSeek-1017, it achieves a score of 73.2 at an average API cost of only USD 0.054 per shot, outperforming the strongest vanilla baseline while reducing total reconstruction time by 53%. We also construct MAVEData-3K, a dataset of 3,000 blockout-video pairs for model training, and will release it publicly. Creators can change viewpoints and character paths, then render the edited scenes to condition video generation. Code is available at https://github.com/yfChang-cv/MAVE.

item.title: Hierarchical Control of Antiphase Synchronization in Biomorphic Spiking Neural Architectures for Locomotor Control [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.22639v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Central pattern generators (CPGs) provide a biologically inspired foundation for adaptive locomotor control, yet systematically characterizing their dynamic regimes in spiking neural networks remains challenging. This study introduces a framework for identifying and stabilizing antiphase synchronization in a biomorphic spiking CPG model embedded in a closed neuromuscular loop. A composite synchronization metric is developed, integrating phase coherence, amplitude balance, and temporal stability. Its performance is evaluated across systematically varied stimulation waveforms and synaptic configurations. Statistical analysis reveals that stimulation type dominates regime determination, with tonic drive yielding the most robust antiphase synchronization. Periodic inputs induce nonlinear saturation and context-dependent network routing. Although synaptic weights alone show limited discriminative power, they significantly modulate robustness within a given stimulation context, with reciprocal Ia interneuron connections emerging as key stabilizers. The proposed composite metric achieves robust antiphase detection, outperforming traditional phase-only measures while preserving biophysical interpretability. These findings establish a statistically validated, hierarchical modeling approach in which external drive defines the operating regime and targeted synaptic configurations fine-tune dynamic stability, providing actionable guidelines for closed-loop neuromechanical controllers and adaptive neuroprosthetic interfaces.

item.title: Check Your Blind Spots: Decision-Guided Perception by Probing the Planner with Hypothetical Objects [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.23030v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Not every perception error changes the planner's action. Yet adaptive-resolution perception chooses where to spend high-resolution computation from image cues, which can neither reliably point to an object that low resolution missed nor tell which objects matter to the planner. We observe that the planner can say where an object would matter before anything is seen: inserting a hypothetical object at a location tests whether its action would change. Decision-Guided Speculative Perception (DGSP) treats the low-resolution scene and its action as a draft and probes the planner in this way to obtain a decision-sensitivity field, the locations where an unseen object would change the action. Only this field and the support, the detections on which the current action rests, are verified at high resolution, repeatedly until the action is stable. For two planner classes, we prove that DGSP returns exactly the action of whole-frame high-resolution perception if crop detections match whole-frame ones and the crops cover the field, conditions that real images meet approximately. On three driving datasets, it reproduces this action on about 98% of frames with about a quarter of the pixels. At the pixel cost of uniform downscaling, it repairs more of the draft's disagreements with this action, brakes falsely less often, and recovers many more of the decision-relevant objects that the draft misses.

item.title: Regularizing Treatment Leakage for LLM-based Uplift Estimation [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.20794v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) provide semantic features for uplift estimation, but treatment-revealing text can induce prediction shortcuts that do not transfer to deployment. We propose LLM-based Uplift Leakage Regularization (LULR) to address this risk. With the LLM encoder frozen, LULR penalizes dependence between the causal head's trainable shared representation and treatment while retaining separate outcome heads. The penalty uses a variational approximation to the contrastive log-ratio upper bound (CLUB) of mutual information, targeting treatment dependence rather than generic parameter shrinkage. Controlled proxy experiments provide exploratory evidence of improved ranking scores under injected treatment information relative to no regularization and the tested weight-decay setting. Structured-only benchmarks show modest, dataset-dependent effects. On an industrial pricing randomized controlled trial, mean offline lift@0.3 is 0.258 for LULR, compared with 0.106 for the same-backbone baseline. A separate one-week online A/B test of the complete deployed pricing policy records 5.45% higher sales volume and 1.91% higher gross merchandise value than the control arm. These short-term policy-level gains do not isolate the regularizer's effect.

item.title: Prioritize, Don't Decide: What We Learned Auditing a Deployed Human-in-the-Loop CV Sorter [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.23359v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A single academic vacancy can draw hundreds of applications, and the first screening round consumes most of a committee's time. We describe a CV Priority Sorter deployed at a national platform for academic vacancies and integrated with its vacancy database. It proposes a reading order for a pile of CVs and leaves every decision to the committee, pairing a frozen multilingual transformer encoder with a per-session linear model that retrains after each label and is discarded when the session ends. It works: on a pool of 300 synthetic CVs, a committee reading in the tool's order reaches 95% of the relevant candidates after half the pile, where an arbitrary order needs almost all of it. This paper is about what we found when we audited that claim, rather than about the system itself. Three findings changed the product. The pool turned out to be sortable by document length alone, which makes precision-style metrics on it uninformative; regenerating it under a shared length budget removes that shortcut and leaves the reading-depth result standing. The four-level agreement score such systems report, ours included, is a binary probability cut at fixed thresholds, so it follows the classifier's confidence rather than its ranking and falls as labels accumulate. And uncertainty sampling, the obvious way to implement a "suggest the next CV" button, leaves model quality intact but raises the committee's total reading load above the no-label baseline, because the CVs it asks about are the ones that would otherwise be skipped. A fourth result shows where to look next: a hosted LLM embedding model lifts zero-label ordinal discrimination from 0.66 to 0.80 under length control, then stops mattering once the session model has two dozen labels; a local cross-encoder matches that cold-start gain without sending data out. We report the fixes each finding forced.

item.title: Tracking Representations in LLM Reasoning Traces for Iterated Games [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.23403v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents achieve state-of-the-art performance across domains through chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning. Despite their ubiquitous use, little is understood about the relationship between the externalized trace and the model's actual computation. We address this by investigating how LLM agents make decisions in iterative games with incomplete information. Using a series of mechanistic interpretability techniques, we find that the model forms and iteratively revises an internal representation of the game throughout the CoT. Once the model prematurely commits to an incorrect belief, it rarely recovers. This failure is manifested in both the literal trace and the layer activations. Ultimately, as multi-agent systems are more prevalent, our work opens the door to a more focused diagnosis of their strategic reasoning errors. For illustrative purposes, we offer an interactive visualizer of our methodology on selected sample traces at https://interp-self.github.io/gametrace/

item.title: From Arraignment to Resolution: Transformer Models of Court Cases [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.23518v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The criminal legal system is composed of many complex decision points, such as which charges are pursued, how bond is determined, plea deal negotiations, and sentencing. Given the profound impact of such decisions, there is a growing need to increase the transparency within this system. While prior machine learning approaches have focused on modeling single decisions (e.g., recidivism), this paper proposes a transformer-based time series model to forecast the outcome of the next proceeding in a case (e.g., charges accepted, bond set, plea deal made, etc.). By modeling a case as an event sequence, we enable a more nuanced analysis to support better oversight and understanding of decision making. We conduct an empirical analysis of thousands of cases using a newly constructed dataset derived from publicly available court records of a mid-sized U.S. city. We fit models that combine textual data from clerk notes with structured information about the defendant, prior charges, and courtroom. Our transformer model achieves $.57$ micro-F1 on a 20-class multi-label task, a significant improvement over several baselines and comparable to a GRU trained on the same input. We demonstrate how the model can be used to provide insights into decision-making and help court observers identify emerging issues within the jurisdiction studied.

item.title: Can LLMs Understand What They Predict? Evaluating Latent Causal Structure Inference in Financial Markets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.23533v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly evaluated through their ability to predict future outcomes, implicitly assuming that predictive success reflects an understanding of the underlying system. However, accurate predictions can often be achieved without recovering the latent mechanisms that generate observable outcomes. To examine this assumption, we introduce LUCID, a benchmark that evaluates whether models can infer latent market structures from event descriptions and historical financial observations. Models generate event-induced causal graphs representing inferred market structure and are evaluated through a reconstruction-based framework. Our evaluation of 6 open-weight and proprietary LLMs shows that adding their generated graphs generally reduces reconstruction quality compared with using historical observations alone, although a few metrics improve. These findings suggest that inferring informative, event-specific market structures from observable evidence remains challenging for the evaluated LLMs.

item.title: Language Models Make New Research Sound Old [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.23546v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Researchers are increasingly using large language models (LLMs) to validate research questions. We find that LLMs make open research questions sound partly studied and overstate what related papers establish. Models recognize most of these overstatements when asked to check the papers' full texts separately. On 40 questions drawn from newly accepted papers, GPT-6-Astra correctly judges 98% to be unstudied, but states that status plainly in only 8% of ordinary answers. All six frontier systems show reporting gaps of 30-90 percentage points. Across 22 models given identical papers, higher capability is associated with more accurate judgments and larger reporting gaps. This reporting failure is asymmetric: models correctly identify studied questions in 88-100% of ordinary answers when we supply the answering papers. To correct this, we build a fixed answer from each model's judgment and separate checks of cited papers. This raises Astra's clear reporting of open status from 8% to 95%, with improvements in all six systems. Finally, we predict reviewers' novelty grades by combining several models' written ratings with a rule learned from graded examples, reaching the performance range reported by Think-Probe-Respond. Unlike TPR, our approach needs no access to model weights or internal activations, so it also works with closed-weight frontier models.

item.title: FutureBench: A Renewable Framework for Evaluating Knowledge-Context Conflict in LLMs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.23601v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Asking a model to check retrieved text can also tell it which source to trust. We introduce FutureBench, a renewable framework for evaluating knowledge-context conflict using timestamped questions, controlled passage triplets, and no-context probes. Across 3,629 questions and six models, Verify (a prompt combining checking with passage priority) raises false-answer adoption in all five models tested on pre-cutoff events, mainly by displacing answers that were correct under Baseline, which allows both passage evidence and model knowledge. On post-cutoff events, only o4-mini increases adoption (+13.7 percentage points). A four-prompt comparison on 902 post-cutoff questions finds that passage priority without checking raises adoption, while moving to Verify lowers it in all five models. Adversarial-Aware, which warns of misleading passages and prioritizes model knowledge, restores 82.5-98.9% of displaced pre-cutoff answers with under one point of change in true-passage accuracy. FutureBench supports repeated evaluation on fixed cohorts and extension to new events as models change.

item.title: Beyond Replacement: Levenshtein Editing for Diffusion Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.23750v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) offer a flexible alternative to autoregressive models, enabling any-order infilling. While most existing decoding methods treat decoded tokens as fixed, some recent models allow previously decoded tokens to be revised only by replacing them with alternative tokens, a paradigm we refer to as replacement-only editing (ROE). Although ROE can correct individual tokens, it is inefficient for sequence shifts caused by missing or extra tokens and struggles when errors occur across many positions. To address these limitations, we propose LED (Levenshtein Editing for Diffusion Language Models), a post-training framework that extends ROE with insertion and deletion, enabling Levenshtein-style refinement of generated sequences. It uses two training designs. First, it reconstructs edit supervision on the fly during supervised fine-tuning using longest-common-subsequence alignment, enabling insertion and deletion learning without manually annotated labels. Second, it adopts multi-stage training, where the state from one stage becomes the input to the next, exposing the model to its earlier errors and enabling it to correct them. When applied to the 16B-parameter LLaDA2.1-Mini Base, LED raises the average score across twelve benchmarks from 54.86 to 57.10 under confidence-guided decoding while increasing tokens per forward from 6.14 to 7.05, whereas under confidence-free decoding it raises the average score from 27.52 to 47.19. We further show that LED achieves higher pass@k at large k than thresholded decoding without editing, demonstrating improved generation diversity and revealing the diversity potential of DLMs without confidence guidance. LED also improves robustness to large block sizes, raising the average score from 36.97 to 51.34 at block size 128. Together, these results suggest that LED supports more robust self-correction in DLMs.

item.title: NarrowSpec: Draft Hidden Width Need Not Match the Target in Speculative Decoding [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.23835v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Speculative decoding is widely used to speed up generation in large language models (LLMs), with a small draft model proposing tokens that one forward pass of the target model verifies. Draft models that read the target's hidden states, such as DFlash and EAGLE-3, typically inherit the target's hidden width. We show that the draft's whole residual stream can run at half or a quarter of that width while largely preserving acceptance. For DFlash, which borrows the target's vocabulary projection, the trained output adapter folds into it, giving one narrower projection with logits unchanged up to floating-point rounding. We test two drafter families, DFlash and EAGLE-3, on two targets, Qwen3-8B (NVFP4) and GPT-OSS-20B (MXFP4), in SGLang on a B200 and a DGX Spark (GB10). At batch size 1 and temperature 0, narrowing the draft to half or a quarter width speeds up end-to-end decoding by 1.06-1.12x on B200 and 1.13-1.44x on GB10. The speedup holds at larger batch sizes. From batch 32 to the largest batch each GPU fits, narrowing reaches up to 1.21x on both GPUs, and no narrow draft is slower than full width.

item.title: Grading Executable Legal Rules Against Independent Records: Transitional Provisions and Korean SME Status [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.24055v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Laws are increasingly turned into programs that decide cases, such as whether a firm was a small or medium enterprise (SME) on a given date, and large language models (LLMs) now write them. The programs are usually graded against answers written by someone who read the same law, so a program can score well by sharing the grader's reading rather than by getting the law right. LexTemporis grades them instead against records of what actually happened: 10,901 firm-years of SME status disclosed by Korean listed companies, with every version of the governing rules. An appendix adds comparison cases from US income tax and German hospital minimum volumes. The date changes outcomes mainly through provisions outside the main statutory text: one transitional provision raises agreement with the disclosures from 83-86% to 89-90%. The disclosures also test the author's reading of a contested provision, favouring it in 130 of 189 firm-years where readings diverge. Four LLMs wrote the rules, given different selections of the law. A pre-registered comparison finds no condition better across all four models. In exploratory analyses, supplying the right provisions looks better graded against the author's reading than against the records: the advantage shrinks for three models (for one, to between a quarter and three-fifths of its size), and per firm-year it is several times larger where the author's reading is wrong, partly by construction, since there reproducing that reading more faithfully must lose. Grading legal programs against the grader's own reading can overstate how well they work.

item.title: Once Upon a Bias: Gender Stereotyping in LLM-Generated Children's Stories [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.24156v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to create stories for children. Since bedtime stories can shape children's perceptions of social roles, this raises concerns about whether LLMs adapt narrative portrayals according to the intended recipient's gender. We conducted a large-scale study to examine gender stereotyping in LLM-generated bedtime stories. Using matched daughter/son prompts and a five-generation design, we analyze 62,873 retained stories from 16 LLMs across 35 country settings and 12 narrator roles. We introduce a multi-level evaluation framework combining context-adjusted lexical rate contrasts, relative stereotype alignment, narrator-recipient interaction analysis, human evaluation, and representation-level interventions to examine both the consistency and interpretability of these differences. Our results reveal systematic differences in narrative framing: son-directed stories emphasize higher agency and lower communion compared to daughter-directed stories. While narrator gender expresses limited moderation on these patterns, high sociability exhibits a more pronounced interaction. Human evaluations demonstrate consistent agreement, although correspondence with lexical measures varies across narrative dimensions. Additionally, hidden-state analyses reveal decodable recipient-gender information. These findings demonstrate persistent yet context-dependent representational disparities in LLM-generated children's stories and motivate narrative-specific bias evaluation beyond short-form benchmarks.

item.title: CounselTraj: Synthesizing Process-Aware Psychological Counseling Dialogues via Dialogue-Act Trajectory Planning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.24168v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The growing demand for psychological counseling has motivated the development of LLM-based systems that support human counselors, but training such systems requires large-scale, high-quality dialogue data. Authentic counseling transcripts are difficult to collect and share because of privacy concerns, making synthetic dialogues an important alternative. However, existing synthetic datasets, despite covering diverse scenarios and client profiles, often consist of brief exchanges and fail to capture session-level counseling processes. We propose CounselTraj, a dialogue-act trajectory planning framework for expanding brief synthetic dialogues into process-aware, session-level psychological counseling dialogues. CounselTraj learns dialogue-act patterns from role-play counseling dialogues produced by human counselors, plans coordinated trajectories for clients and counselors, and uses them as flexible guidance for long-form dialogue generation. Experiments across three Chinese synthetic counseling datasets show that CounselTraj produces more complete and coherent sessions with higher-quality counselor interventions than both direct expansion and expansion with randomly sampled trajectories. Based on CounselTraj, we construct CounselTrajD, a dataset containing over 10K process-guided Chinese psychological counseling dialogues, and use it to train CounselTrajLM for counseling response generation. Evaluations at both the response and session levels show that CounselTrajLM outperforms publicly available Chinese counseling models in response quality, therapeutic understanding and intervention, and counseling-process coherence and progress. Our code and model are publicly available at https://github.com/UEC-InabaLab/CounselTraj.

item.title: LoopCache: Accelerating Long-Context Self-Speculative Decoding for Looped Transformers [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.24301v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Looped Transformers achieve large effective depth with compact models by repeatedly applying a weight-shared block across R recurrent steps, each maintaining a loop-specific key-value (KV) cache. To accelerate sequential loop execution, recent wave-style self-speculative methods like WaveFront Decoding (WFD) and LoopSpec pipeline draft and target tokens across loops in a single step. However, they face two critical limitations. First, they draft only at fixed loops and ignore intermediate prediction changes, wasting computation on stale trajectories. Second, batching tokens from different loops loads up to Rx the KV cache per step, severely amplifying memory traffic in long-context scenarios. To address these challenges, we propose LoopCache, an efficient self-speculative decoding framework for long-context Looped Transformers. Based on the correlation between prediction switches and output confidence, LoopCache introduces confidence-guided dynamic draft updating to refine drafts in flight across all intermediate loops. Furthermore, LoopCache employs a cyclic loop KV cache strategy that rotates through loop-specific KV caches, restricting per-step KV traffic to a single loop while batching tokens at the nearest matching cycle for lossless verification. By also selectively retaining independent KV caches for a few loop-sensitive shallow layers, LoopCache improves acceptance rates with negligible overhead. Experiments show that LoopCache achieves average 10.25x and 14.56x speedup over WFD and LoopSpec.

item.title: Nothing to Declare: Steering a single neuron increases concealment in AI teams [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.24475v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent research suggests that individual neurons can have interpretable roles in AI behaviour. In Qwen3.5-4B, steering along one neuron's output direction increased decisions to conceal information more in teams than alone across five scenarios, even when teammates provided no messages. When all members participated and received steering, collective concealment increased in four scenarios, while inter-agent messaging helped temper concealment under steering. Moreover, removing the neuron's contribution had negligible effects. Collective settings can therefore change how an internal intervention affects AI behaviour.

item.title: MECI: Multi-Element Collaborative Interaction for Multimodal Entity Linking [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.24522v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multimodal Entity Linking (MEL) aims to disambiguate mentions in multimodal contexts by grounding them to specific entities in a knowledge base. A pivotal challenge in MEL is capturing multi-level correspondences: the semantic consistency between mention-entity pairs and the complementary correlations across modalities. However, existing methods often suffer from element dominance due to their reliance on coupled interactions or coarse global aggregations. In response, we propose the Multi-Element Collaborative Interaction (MECI) framework. First, to capture multi-element mention-entity correspondences, we develop a Multi-view Experts Network that leverages a "divide-and-conquer" strategy for decoupled feature learning to mitigate element dominance, supported by a KL-guided routing mechanism that governs expert specialization and collaboration. Furthermore, to model cross-modal complementary correlations, we propose a Hierarchical Multimodal Interaction Module, where a dynamic modality-aware weighting network refines interactions across hierarchical semantic levels, thereby integrating multi-granular evidence to counteract element dominance. Finally, we incorporate a generative semantic refinement stage that utilizes large language models for zero-shot re-ranking. Extensive experiments on WikiDiverse, RichpediaMEL, and WikiMEL show that MECI consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, improving Hits@1 by 1.95%, 7.30%, and 2.31%, respectively.

item.title: Do Frontier Model Ingredients Add Up? A Replicated Factorial Study of Small Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.24540v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Building a small language model requires choosing which published improvements to combine. We compare five changes in the same model, using the same data and training budget. We test selected combinations and repeat each one with a second random seed.
